# zubin

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zubin/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zubin/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zubin/main/.github/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zubin/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Every binary format, from an image header to a market data feed to a C struct
dumped to disk, is specified the same way: a table of fields, each with a name, a
type, a width and an offset. Base R reads such data one `readBin()` call at a time,
loops over the records itself, has no unsigned 32-bit integer and no half-precision
float, and reads an 8-byte integer silently wrong once it outgrows 32 bits.

zubin lets you write the table down once, as a *layout*, and then read or write any
number of records in one call.

* **Describe once, read millions.** A layout is one string,
  `"<id:u32 ts:i64 price:f64 side:u8"`, and `bin_unpack()` turns a raw vector into a
  data frame of every record in it, one tight loop per field.
* **Every type a format uses.** Integers from 8 to 128 bits, signed and unsigned;
  `f16`, `bf16`, `f32` and `f64`; complex numbers; booleans; fixed bytes and
  strings; arrays; padding; either byte order, per field; and C struct alignment.
* **Exact, or an error.** Nothing is silently rounded, wrapped or truncated. A
  64-bit integer that a double cannot hold, or a value too large for its field, is an
  error that names the field and the record.
* **Writing too.** `bin_pack()` and `bin_encode()` are the inverses, and a byte
  builder appends without quadratic copying, up to a hard cap.
* **A C library underneath.** The same buffers, cursors and kernels are a
  header-only C99 library that other packages use through `LinkingTo` alone.

## Installation

``` r
install.packages("zubin")
```

or the development version from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zubin")
```

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zubin)
```

**Read a real header.** A PNG file opens with an 8-byte signature and then an `IHDR`
chunk, big-endian, as its specification lays it out. That table, written down, reads
the image's size from the file R just wrote:

```{r}
png_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
png(png_file, width = 640, height = 480)
plot(pressure)
invisible(dev.off())

ihdr <- bin_layout(">x8 length:u32 type:s4 width:u32 height:u32 depth:u8 colour:u8")
bin_unpack(readBin(png_file, "raw", 64), ihdr, n = 1)
```

**The types base R lacks.** `readBin()` has no unsigned 32-bit integers and no half
floats; zubin decodes both, in either byte order:

```{r}
x <- as.raw(c(0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff))
readBin(x, "integer", size = 4, signed = FALSE)
bin_decode(x, "u32")

# half-precision floats, as machine-learning weights are stored
bin_decode(as.raw(c(0x00, 0x3c, 0x00, 0xc0, 0x00, 0x7c)), "f16")
```

**Exact, or an error.** `readBin()` reads the 8-byte integer 2^32 as 0, without a
word. zubin reads it exactly, and refuses a value above 2^53, which has no exact
double, naming the record rather than handing back a neighbouring number
(`int64 = "integer64"` returns the exact bits instead):

```{r, error = TRUE}
counts <- bin_encode(c(2^32, 2^53 + 2), "u64")
readBin(counts, "integer", size = 8, n = 2)
bin_decode(counts[1:8], "u64")
bin_decode(counts, "u64")
```

**Take a number apart.** A double is a sign bit, an 11-bit exponent and a 52-bit
fraction. Encoded and read back as two unsigned words, its fields come out exactly,
and `0.1` turns out to be `7205759403792794 / 2^56`, a little more than a tenth:

```{r}
w <- bin_unpack(bin_encode(c(1, 0.1, -2.5), "f64", endian = "big"), ">hi:u32 lo:u32")
bits <- function(v, from, width) (v %/% 2^from) %% 2^width
parts <- data.frame(sign = bits(w$hi, 31, 1), exponent = bits(w$hi, 20, 11) - 1023,
                    fraction = bits(w$hi, 0, 20) * 2^32 + w$lo)
format(parts, scientific = FALSE)
(2^52 + parts$fraction[2]) / 2^56 == 0.1
```

The same bytes read as two types give Quake III's fast inverse square root: a
float's bits read as an integer, halved, subtracted from a magic number and read
back as a float, then one step of Newton's method:

```{r}
x <- c(0.25, 2, 10)
i <- bin_decode(bin_encode(x, "f32"), "u32")
y <- bin_decode(bin_encode(0x5f3759df - i %/% 2, "u32"), "f32")
rbind(fast = y * (1.5 - 0.5 * x * y^2), exact = 1 / sqrt(x))
```

**A million records in one call.** Packing a data frame and unpacking it again is
one call each way, and the round trip is exact:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
rec <- bin_layout("<id:i32 price:f64 qty:i16 x2")
trades <- data.frame(id = 1:1e6, price = round(runif(1e6, 90, 110), 2),
                     qty = sample(1:500, 1e6, replace = TRUE))
bytes <- bin_pack(rec, trades)
length(bytes)
identical(bin_unpack(bytes, rec), trades)
```

**Write a file format.** A builder collects a header and the records after it, and
`bin_hexdump()` shows the bytes with their 0-based offsets:

```{r}
hdr <- bin_layout(">magic:u32 version:u16 count:u32")
b <- bin_builder()
bin_put(b, bin_pack(hdr, magic = 0x5A55424E, version = 1, count = 2))
bin_put(b, bin_pack(rec, head(trades, 2)))
bin_hexdump(bin_take(b))
```

Every function is prefixed `bin_`, and offsets are 0-based everywhere, as in every
format specification.

## Learn more

* [Structured binary data with zubin](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zubin/articles/zubin.html),
  the getting-started guide: layouts, a WAV file written and read back, C structs,
  arrays, 64-bit integers and errors.
* [Recipes](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zubin/articles/recipes.html): one block of
  bytes, many readings, from a Nasdaq ITCH feed to a UUID, a Windows timestamp and an
  RGB565 pixel.
* [The C API](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zubin/articles/c-api.html), for package
  authors: the `LinkingTo` recipe, the cursor, the record kernels, and buffers owned
  by R.
* The [reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zubin/reference/), with the
  full type table under `?bin_layout`.

## Related work

zubin's integer loads and stores, half-float conversions and UTF-8 validation come
from [zufast](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zufast). Python's
[`struct`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html) module and the structured
dtypes of NumPy are the nearest equivalents in other languages.
